strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely gap: existing datasets either offer scale/semantics without geometry or geometry without dynamic real-world content. The proposed resource (2.7M clips, 7,089 hours, ~127M annotated frames with camera poses, depth, dynamic masks, structured captions, and serialized motion instructions) is, per Table 1, substantially larger than comparable dynamic datasets with geometric annotations (e.g., DynPose-100K at 6.8M frames, Stereo4D at 10M frames, Sekai at ~600 hours).

The curation pipeline is clearly documented and decomposed (filtering, geometric annotation, motion instruction decomposition, semantic captioning), with concrete thresholds, tool choices (MegaSaM upgraded with UniDepth v2 / Depth Anything v2, SAM2-based dynamic segmentation, scenedetect modifications), and compute costs reported, which supports reproducibility of the pipeline.

The camera-pose-grounded caption refinement (Fig. 8-9) is a sensible and somewhat novel design: using estimated trajectories as a geometric prior to correct VLM motion-direction errors is a practical contribution beyond plain MLLM captioning.

The paper provides useful dataset analysis: distribution statistics over motion directions (Fig. 10), scene tags (Fig. 12), trajectory metrics (MoveDist, RotAngle, TrajTurns in Fig. 13), and a same-pipeline comparison against Panda-70M that demonstrates its filters and manual curation yield a more motion-rich corpus.

The proposed SpatialVID-HQ subset with balanced motion/category distributions, and the derived controlled-vocabulary motion instructions, are directly usable for camera-controllable video generation and navigation-style training.
weaknesses: The most consequential weakness: the abstract claims the data 'directly foster[s] improved model generalization and performance,' yet the paper contains zero downstream experiments. No video generation, camera-control, reconstruction, or navigation model is trained or fine-tuned on SpatialVID, and no benchmark results are reported. The central utility claim is therefore unsupported by evidence in the manuscript.

Annotations are pseudo-ground truth from MegaSaM and depth models, but their accuracy is never quantitatively validated. Fig. 6 is a purely qualitative trajectory visualization; the proposed metrics (MoveDist, RotAngle, TrajTurns) measure motion statistics, not annotation correctness. There is no evaluation on sequences with known pose (e.g., held-out held-up-camera footage or benchmark splits), no reported pose-estimation success/failure rates across the corpus, and no accuracy figures for depth or dynamic masks. The abstract's phrase 'ground-truth camera motion' is inaccurate and should be softened.

Dataset construction is hard to reproduce at the level described: 21,789 hours of YouTube video were manually screened, and the captioning pipeline depends on commercial/API models (Gemini-2.0-flash, Qwen3-30B). The paper does not discuss licensing/redistribution rights for YouTube-derived content or for pseudo-labels generated with proprietary models, which matters for a resource intended for community release.

Evaluation of the semantic annotations is weak: caption quality is assessed mainly via caption-length statistics (Fig. 11), a word cloud, and cherry-picked examples (Fig. 9, 14). There is no human evaluation, no controlled comparison against baseline VLM captions, and no measurement of caption-pose consistency over the corpus (the Fig. 9 correction could be an anecdote rather than a systematic improvement).

Scene and motion diversity is narrower than the 'open-scenario' framing suggests: source videos come from a small set of keyword queries (walk, tour, drone, etc.), the motion distribution is heavily imbalanced (33.3% 'Forward' in the full set; HQ rebalancing raises several minor categories but 'Forward' remains dominant), and the exclusion criteria (no dominant moving foreground, no zoom-only, sufficient parallax) inherently bias the corpus toward smooth, landscape/tour-style footage that may not represent general dynamic scenes.

Several methodological details are under-specified or unvalidated: the VMAF motion-score range '2.0 to 14.0' is stated without justification or sensitivity analysis; filtering thresholds are given but their effect on final data quality is not ablated; and the 'acceleration-based' plausibility check for trajectories is mentioned but never quantified (e.g., what fraction of clips are rejected).

The manuscript has notable writing/consistency issues (e.g., Fig. 4 shows 29,966 videos / 19,982 hours while Sec. 3.1.1 reports 33,443 videos / 21,789 hours without reconciliation; Table 1 and Fig. 2 do not clarify how 'Pose Wrong' vs. 'Pose Estimation Failed' clips are detected), and there is no defined train/val/test split or standardized benchmark protocol, limiting immediate comparability for follow-up work.

strengths: Scale and annotation richness: the dataset is genuinely large (2.7M clips / 7,089 hours of dynamic real-world video with per-frame camera poses, depth, dynamic masks, structured captions, and motion instructions), and Table 1 supports the claim that this is the largest resource of its kind relative to prior datasets like DynPose100K, Stereo4D, and the concurrent Sekai.

The structured captioning pipeline (Fig. 8-9) is a thoughtful design: injecting estimated camera poses as geometric priors into LLM-based caption refinement is a concrete, novel mechanism for improving the spatial consistency of video captions, and Fig. 9 gives a convincing qualitative example (correcting a left/right motion error).

The paper is transparent about the curation procedure: hardware costs (e.g., 69,120 GPU-hours for MegaSaM annotation, 9B caption tokens), filtering thresholds, clip statistics, and failure modes (Pose Wrong / Pose Estimation Failed in Fig. 2) are documented, which aids reproducibility of the pipeline.
The comparison against Panda-70M processed through the identical pipeline (Fig. 13) is a reasonable controlled experiment showing the value of the manual, motion-first curation strategy.
The dedicated HQ subset (1,146 hours) with balanced motion/category distributions is a useful deliverable for training and evaluation.
weaknesses: No downstream validation whatsoever. The abstract claims the data 'directly foster improved model generalization and performance,' but the paper contains zero training experiments (no camera-controllable video generation, no reconstruction, no instruction-following fine-tuning). For a dataset paper whose core motivation is enabling such models, this is the single most consequential gap: the claimed utility is asserted, not demonstrated.

The geometric annotations are pseudo-ground-truth from MegaSaM, and the paper provides no quantitative accuracy assessment of them. Fig. 6 is purely qualitative trajectory visualization; there is no evaluation against any benchmark with reliable pose ground truth (e.g., TUM dynamic sequences, Princeton365, or synthetic data with known poses) for the upgraded MegaSaM+UniDepth v2 pipeline actually used. Since the entire dataset's value rests on annotation quality, this is a material weakness, not a presentation issue.

The proposed validation criterion for trajectories (detecting non-physical acceleration fluctuations) is ad hoc and circular: it measures smoothness of the estimator's own output, not correctness. Similarly, MoveDist/RotAngle/TrajTurns are dataset statistics, not quality measures.

Severe copyright/licensing and distribution uncertainty. The data is scraped from YouTube (33,443 videos) and only 'manually screened'; the paper does not address whether, or under what terms, the videos themselves can be redistributed. This materially affects the dataset's usefulness as a community resource, which is its entire contribution.

Scale claims are inflated by construction: 21,789 hours of raw video yield 7,089 hours, and the 2.7M clips come from only ~30K source videos, so effective diversity is far lower than the clip count suggests; many clips are highly redundant segments of the same footage. The paper does not report deduplication statistics or near-duplicate analysis.

The comparison to Panda-70M is a strawman in places: Panda-70M was not designed for geometric annotation, and 'over 80% cannot be reconstructed by MegaSaM' partly reflects the estimator's limits on static content rather than dataset quality alone.

Writing quality is below the bar for a camera-ready paper: grammatical errors throughout ('Recent advances has developed,' 'a dataset consists of,' 'These modifications improves'), inconsistent naming (SpatialVID-hq vs SpatialVID-HQ), and a citation rendered as '(Authors, 2020)' for PaddleOCR.

strengths: The dataset is substantial and addresses a real gap: existing spatially-annotated datasets (RealEstate10K, CO3D, DynPose100K, Stereo4D) are limited in scale or restricted to static/object-centric content, while large video datasets lack geometric grounding. SpatialVID's 7,089 hours / 2.7M clips / 127M frames of real-world dynamic content with camera poses, depth, dynamic masks, structured captions, and motion instructions is, to the authors' credible knowledge, the largest resource of its kind, including a 1,146-hour balanced HQ subset.

The curation pipeline is well documented and reproducible in spirit: motion-keyword YouTube collection with explicit exclusion criteria, scene segmentation with a modified PySceneDetect (interval-based multi-frame comparison for fades), and multi-criteria filtering (CLIP+MLP aesthetics with a stated 4.0 threshold, luminance range [20,140] with formula, PaddleOCR text-area ratio <30%, VMAF motion score 2.0–14.0). Concrete thresholds and tool versions are provided rather than vague descriptions.

The paper is honest about the limitations of its annotation backbone: it explicitly discusses MegaSaM's failure modes (dominant moving objects, collinear motion, variable focal length) and mitigates them by upgrading to UniDepth v2 / Depth Anything v2, and by integrating SAM2 with adaptive thresholding and contour-based anchoring to improve dynamic masks.

The structured captioning pipeline (Gemini-2.0-flash for visual parsing, then Qwen3-30B-A3B with camera poses as a geometric prior) is a sensible design, and Fig. 9 gives a convincing qualitative example of pose-informed correction of a VLM's misidentified camera motion direction.

The comparison with Panda-70M processed through the identical pipeline (Fig. 13) is a fair, controlled analysis across aesthetics, luminance, motion, RotAngle, MoveDist, and TrajTurns, and the proposed trajectory statistics (MoveDist, RotAngle, TrajTurns) are simple but useful dataset-level metrics. Coverage statistics (Figs. 4, 10, 12) demonstrate genuine diversity in motion types and scene attributes.
weaknesses: The central utility claim is not empirically validated. The abstract and conclusion assert that the dataset 'directly foster[s] improved model generalization and performance,' yet the paper contains no downstream training experiments (e.g., camera-controlled video generation, pose estimation, navigation models) on SpatialVID or SpatialVID-HQ. For a dataset paper of this ambition, at least one fine-tuning/ablation showing measurable benefit over a baseline dataset would substantially strengthen the case; without it, the utility claim rests on scale and annotation richness alone.

The geometric annotations are pseudo-ground-truth with no quantitative accuracy assessment. MegaSaM's superiority over DROID-SLAM, COLMAP, Fast3R, MonST3R, and VGGT is shown only qualitatively (Fig. 6 trajectory visualizations) with no numbers, and the final poses/depths are never evaluated against any ground truth or held-out benchmark. The proposed acceleration-based validation for trajectory plausibility is mentioned but no failure-rate or error statistics on the actual 2.7M clips are reported, leaving annotation quality unquantified.

Caption quality is likewise unverified beyond length statistics (Fig. 11) and single examples; there is no human evaluation, factual-consistency check at scale, or comparison of the structured captions' downstream usefulness versus vanilla VLM captions.

Reproducibility and access details are incomplete: no release URL, license, or data card is given, and copyright/ethical considerations around large-scale YouTube scraping and redistribution are not discussed. The scale of 'manual screening' of 21,789 hours is also not characterized (annotator count, inter-rater agreement, screening time), making the most labor-intensive pipeline stage difficult to assess or reproduce.

Several internal inconsistencies and polish issues remain: resolution is stated as 720P clips in Sec. 1 but transcoding to 1920x1080 in Sec. 3.1.2; typos ('dataaset', 'Recent advances has developed', 'We processe'); some references to figures/text are imprecise (e.g., Fig. 13f is called 'Arc Nums' while Sec. 4.1 refers to 'Arc Nums' statistics that are never formally defined); and Table 1 mixes confirmed and approximate frame counts without a source for third-party entries.

Comparison with the concurrent Sekai dataset (600 hours) is mentioned but brief; a more careful head-to-head of annotation types and quality would better position the contribution relative to the closest competing effort.
